human_tolerance.notes: 'This species can occasionally be found in urban or suburban areas. However, they seem to prefer areas with less human activity and are most likely to be found in park-like settings in such developed areas, unlike eastern and western screech owls... which may regularly occur in busy suburban settings.' In Wisconsin urban nests hatched a month earlier than rural ones, attributed to protection from wind and cold, and Winnipeg birds began nesting five to six weeks early on the urban heat island. light_max and flight_distance_m are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: 'In most of North America, courtship is from October to December and mates are chosen by December to January.' The male hoots emphatically for about a month or six weeks towards the end of the year while the period in which females also hoot is usually only a week to ten days; he leans over with his tail folded or cocked and his white throat puffed 'to look like a ball', and may convince the female by bringing her freshly caught prey.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: 'Usually, territorial hooting decreases in February or March at the onset of egg laying', and 'all mated great horned owls are permanent residents of their territories'. Males select the nesting site and bring the female's attention to it by flying to the nest and stomping on it.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Some of the earliest-breeding birds in North America. 'There are usually 2 eggs per clutch, but clutches range in size from 1 to 6 eggs (over 3 is uncommon, over 4 is very rare).' Both parents incubate once the eggs are laid. The stage at which eggs are laid is variable: late November to early January in southern Florida, late December to early February in the southeast, and early February onwards from southern California to northern Louisiana - which brackets interior Colorado. The first nightly food delivery typically occurs soon after dark.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Nestlings weigh 34.7 g at birth on average and gain about 33 g a day for the first four weeks, reaching 800 g (males) to 1,000 g (females) by 25-29 days, covered at hatching in whitish grey down that gives way to cinnamon-buff juvenile downy plumage. 'During their initial dispersal in fall, juvenile owls have a high mortality rate, frequently more than 50%', and Yukon juvenile survival in the 9 weeks after dispersal fell from 80% to 23.2% over three years as food supply destabilised.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: 'Unmated and younger birds move freely in search of company and a territory and leave regions with little food in winter.' This is dispersal rather than migration, and the fraction is judgement - the source gives no proportion.

vocalizations.description: The song is 'normally a low-pitched but loud ho-ho-hoo hoo hoo (or also transcribed as bu-bubu booh, who-hoo-ho-oo or who-ho-o-o, whoo-hoo-o-o, whoo)' and can last four or five syllables; resonant, and described as variously 'solemn' and 'terrifying'. The female's call is higher and rises in pitch at the end. 'At dusk, the owl utters a few calls before flying to a more open sing-post... to deliver song', and 'calling seems to peak after rather than before midnight'.

When disturbed or angered at the nest the bird gives 'an indescribable assemblage of hoots, chuckles, screeches, and squawks, given so rapidly and disconnectedly that the effect is both startling and amusing', including a growling krrooo-ooo pair, a laughing whar, whah, wha-a-a-a-ah, a high-pitched ank, ank, ank, a cat-like meee-owwwwww and a hawk-like ke-yah, ke-yah. These sounds 'frequently preced[e] an attack on an interloping human or other animal'.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 20044 to 'Great Horned Owl'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685). Wikidata P2050 also carries a wingspan of 1.34 m, consistent with the 91-153 cm range and 122 cm mean quoted from Wikipedia.

range.note: 'They are distributed throughout most of North America and very spottily in Central America and then down into South America south to upland regions of Argentina, Bolivia and Peru... It is absent or rare from southern Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica to Panama... The species is also absent from the West Indies, Haida Gwaii, and almost all off-shore islands in the Americas'. The country and state lists are an approximation of that description and are not exhaustive; the South American countries listed are those the source names directly. elevation_m is the sourced 3,300 m ceiling 'in the Rockies', which is the range the locale sits in.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes: the owl 'can fly at a very low speed for the size of the species, as slow as 2 miles per hour when they are gliding on breezes' and makes 'great use of secrecy and stealth', roosting in large trees by day and walking about on powerful legs and talons. Glide is a locomotion mode here because the species' low-speed flight is explicitly gliding; Powered is retained for the silent flapping flight.

traits.nest_type.note: Judgement mapping: 'Like all owls, great horned owls do not build their own nest' but 'tend to examine an area for an abandoned nest, generally from larger birds like hawks, and take over the nest for raising their own young', with 'Many nests... in cavernous hollows of dead trees or their branches', cliff ledges, small caves, rock shelters, boulders, railroad cuts and low bushes. The schema's enum has no 'abandoned raptor nest' option; Cavity is chosen as the closest fit because tree hollows are the most frequently named site, and the abandoned-stick-nest case is carried in habitat.resources as nest_platform.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~1.4 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Medium band.

traits.mass_kg.note: Mean of the two sex means the source gives: 1,608 g for females and 1,224 g for males, giving 1,416 g. 'Females are somewhat larger than males', and size varies by subspecies across the range.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: From the male mean of 1,224 g (the lightest typical bird) to the stated subspecies maximum of 2,503 g. The source gives no overall minimum or maximum beyond those figures.

traits.length_m.note: 'Adult great horned owls range in length from 43 to 64 cm, with an average of 55 cm' - the stated average is used directly rather than the midpoint, because the source gives one.

traits.wingspan_m.note: 'possess a wingspan of 91 to 153 cm, with an average of 122 cm' - the stated average is used directly, and Wikidata P2050 independently records 1.34 m.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Great horned owls seem to be the most long-lived owl in North America... almost 29 years being the highest age for an owl recorded in North America. In captivity, the record for the longest lived great horned owl was 50 years. A more typical top lifespan of a great horned owl is approximately 13 years.' The typical figure is used, as the schema asks for a typical lifespan; the record figures are recorded here.

traits.diet.note: The Prey and trophic ecology section and its subsections (Rodents, Lagomorphs, Other mammals, Birds, Other prey, Urban vs rural diet) give the prey list in detail without percentages: rodents, lagomorphs, other mammals, birds up to the size of a great blue heron, plus reptiles, amphibians, insects and, rarely, carrion. Shares are judgement, with the vertebrate tag covering both the small mammal prey and the larger kills, since the schema's diet block has no finer key for them. The source also records the bird-hunting consequence - 'crows sometimes congregate from considerable distances to mob owls and caw angrily at them for hours on end' - which is why Defense is Mob.

traits.social.note: 'Pairs typically breed together year after year and may mate for life, although they associate with each other more loosely when their young become mostly independent.' The species 'was once thought to be strictly monogamous, but recent analysis indicates one male may mate with two females simultaneously'.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Generally great horned owls are active at night, although in some areas they may be active in the late afternoon or early morning', and the species makes 'silent flight'.

traits.defense.note: 'few species press attacks on the owl's nests due to the ferocious defensive abilities of the parents', and the disturbance calls 'frequently preced[e] an attack on an interloping human or other animal'.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: it uses city parks but 'seem[s] to prefer areas with less human activity', nests in taller urban trees 'due to the fact that urban areas have large trees used for ornamentation', and the higher nesting 'was attributed to human avoidance', so a middling-high wariness value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. small_vertebrate, vertebrate, invertebrate and carrion tags come from the Prey and trophic ecology section; perch from the daytime roosting behaviour in large trees and on rock outcrops; nest_platform from the abandoned raptor and crow nests it takes over. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: 'They prefer areas where open habitats, which they often hunt in, and woods, where they tend to roost and nest, are juxtaposed'; by day it roosts in large trees including snags and hollows, crevices or small rock caves, or dense shrubbery, and 'Pine and other coniferous trees may be preferred where available since they are particularly dense and provide cover throughout the year'.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat and Urban vs rural nesting sections, quoted at length in the field, including the Wisconsin and Winnipeg urban-nesting findings. Adapter rather than Exploiter, because the source explicitly contrasts the species with the screech owls that 'may regularly occur in busy suburban settings'. light_max and flight_distance_m are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'All mated great horned owls are permanent residents of their territories, but unmated and younger birds move freely in search of company and a territory and leave regions with little food in winter' - local movement and dispersal rather than migration, so ActiveYearRound was used.

seasonal.phases.note: October-December courtship and mate choice by December-January, territorial hooting tapering from February-March at egg laying, early breeding with the quoted clutch and range of laying dates, nestling growth and weight gain, autumn dispersal with the quoted juvenile mortality, and year-round territoriality. The nesting and breeding phases are tagged US-CO because the locale that prompted this record is in Colorado; the source gives laying dates by broad region and the early-February-to-northern-Louisiana band is the one that brackets interior Colorado. Day-of-month boundaries other than October, December, January, February and March are judgement. The flocking phase is dispersal rather than flocking in the social sense and carries a judgement fraction.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Reproduction and Longevity sections: 'The young weigh 34.7 g (1.22 oz) at birth on average and can gain about 33 g (1.2 oz) a day for the first four weeks of life, with typical weights in the range of 800 or 1,000 g by 25-29 days for males and females, respectively. When first hatched the young are covered in whitish gray down, with some brownish about the wings.' duration_days 200 is derived from that four-week nestling phase plus the autumn dispersal period for which the source gives 'frequently more than 50%' mortality; scale 0.4 is judgement for a recently fledged bird.

vocalizations.hoot.note: Calls section, quoted closely in the field: the song, its alternative transcriptions, the four-to-five syllable length, the higher and rising female call, the dusk sing-post behaviour and the after-midnight peak. season_months follows the courtship and territorial-hooting window the source dates (October to March), during which the male hoots for about a month or six weeks and the female for only a week to ten days.

vocalizations.squawk.note: Calls section: the 'indescribable assemblage of hoots, chuckles, screeches, and squawks' given when disturbed or angered at the nest, with the individual notes listed in the field, 'frequently preceding an attack on an interloping human or other animal'. It is the alarm slot of the shared program.

look.note: Description section: 'The underparts of the species are usually light with some brown horizontal barring; the upper parts and upper wings are generally a mottled brown usually bearing heavy, complex, darker markings. All subspecies are darkly barred to some extent along the sides. A variable-sized white patch is seen on the throat... The skin of the feet and legs... is black. Even tropical great horned owls have feathered legs and feet. The bill is dark gunmetal-gray, as are the talons', with a facial disc 'reddish, brown, or gray... demarked by a dark rim culminating in bold, blackish side brackets', and 'The iris is yellow, except in the amber-eyed South American great horned owl'. The palette maps the mottled brown onto the body, the barred light underparts onto the breast, the darker complex markings onto the wings and tail, the gunmetal bill onto the beak and the yellow iris onto the eye. The plumicorn 'horns' and the facial disc have no separate part in the biped_winged body plan and are not modelled; proportions are authored judgement from the 'barrel-shaped body, a large head, and broad wings', the large head_scale and the 'relatively short' tail.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, used here for a very large nocturnal raptor rather than a small songbird: flee_m 40 is the longest flight distance in this locale's cast, matching an owl that flushes at tens of metres; food_tag is small_vertebrate, the dominant prey group; song_cooldown_s 30 matches the once-a-month-or-six-weeks male hooting pattern rather than a per-minute song; nest_m1/nest_m2 span the earliest-of-any-North-American-breeder window the source describes, February to April.
